#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when a version range picks something you never tested*
This scenario demonstrates version ranges in sbt, and why a build that uses them resolves differently depending on when and where it runs.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA["lib-a:[1.0.0,2.0.0)"]
    LibA -.->|today| V1[lib-a:1.0.0]
```

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="s9-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
The range `[1.0.0,2.0.0)` always gives the latest 1.x, so you get patches for free and nothing breaks.

#### ! Actual
Today it resolves `1.0.0`, because that is the only 1.x in the repository. The day someone publishes `1.1.0`, every build that has not cached the old answer resolves `1.1.0` instead, with no change to your source. Ranges make the repository's contents part of your build input.

#### ! Why
Coursier queries `maven-metadata.xml` for the artifact, lists the available versions and selects the highest one inside the range. Nothing is recorded about which version it chose, so two machines with different cache states, or one machine on two days, can disagree. Coursier also caches metadata with a time-to-live, so a CI server and a developer laptop routinely see different answers for the same range.

#### ! Fix
*   **Pin exact versions** for everything that ships. Let a bot (Scala Steward, Renovate) propose upgrades as pull requests instead of letting the resolver take them silently.
*   **Lock** if ranges must stay: the `sbt-dependency-lock` plugin freezes the resolved graph (SB11).
*   **Keep ranges to test tooling** where a surprise upgrade costs little.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Ranges on `Test`-only dependencies.
* MEDIUM Ranges on internal libraries under strict semantic versioning that your own team controls.
* HIGH Ranges on external libraries in production builds: non-deterministic resolution and `AbstractMethodError` on the next automated redeploy.

#### ! Control
Treat a range in `build.sbt` as a code smell in review. If one is needed, pair it with a committed lock file and a CI check that resolution has not drifted.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `sbt dependencyTree`

**What to look for:** The concrete version Coursier chose for `lib-a`, which is not in your build file.

**Conclusion:** Ranges trade reproducibility for freshness.

#### ! Scales
At scale, ranges are how a build "worked yesterday and fails today" with no commit in between. Organisations that allow them typically do so only inside a locked build, so the lock file, not the repository, decides what ships.

#### ! Takeaway
A range delegates the version decision to the repository on the day of the build. Pin or lock before you ship.

#### ! Wild

A well-known failure mode with version ranges occurs when CI resolves a newly published dependency that developer machines have not yet seen. sbt uses [Coursier](https://get-coursier.io/) for resolution, which keeps its own local cache separate from Maven's, with its own metadata refresh policy. A range like `[1.0,2.0)` can therefore resolve to different concrete versions on different machines, and the build fails without any source change. sbt has no built-in locking; the third-party [sbt-dependency-lock](https://github.com/stringbean/sbt-dependency-lock) plugin can freeze resolution results to prevent this drift.
